name: Autosomal recessive spastic ataxia of Charlevoix-Saguenay (SACS)

clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive early-onset (typically childhood) disorder combining progressive cerebellar ataxia, spasticity and a peripheral neuropathy
Caused by biallelic mutations in SACS encoding the large chaperone protein sacsin
Originally described in the Charlevoix-Saguenay region of Quebec through a founder effect but now recognised worldwide
A characteristic finding is retinal nerve fibre hypermyelination (thickened, striated peripapillary fibres) visible on fundoscopy and optical coherence tomography
The combination of pyramidal spasticity with cerebellar signs gives a spastic-ataxic gait, and a length-dependent sensorimotor neuropathy adds distal wasting and areflexia
MRI shows cerebellar (superior vermian) atrophy together with characteristic linear pontine hypointensities and, often, thickening of the pons
Nerve conduction studies confirm the associated demyelinating or axonal neuropathy
Management is supportive, with physiotherapy, spasticity management, orthoses, and mobility and falls support
reference.pathophysiology: ARSACS is caused by biallelic mutations in SACS, encoding sacsin, a very large multidomain protein with chaperone-like activity that is important for protein quality control and mitochondrial dynamics, and is highly expressed in cerebellar Purkinje cells. Loss of functional sacsin impairs handling of misfolded proteins and disturbs the mitochondrial network and neurofilament organisation, leading to degeneration of Purkinje cells, corticospinal tracts and peripheral nerves. This combined central and peripheral pathology produces the hallmark triad of cerebellar ataxia, pyramidal spasticity and peripheral neuropathy, with the retinal nerve fibre hypermyelination reflecting the disorder's effect on the retinal nerve fibre layer.
additionalDifferentials: Friedreich ataxia and other early-onset recessive ataxias
Hereditary spastic paraplegias with cerebellar or neuropathic features
Other autosomal recessive cerebellar ataxias with neuropathy
Mitochondrial disorders combining ataxia, spasticity and neuropathy
Metachromatic leukodystrophy and other leukodystrophies with neuropathy
Vitamin E deficiency ataxia and other treatable recessive ataxias
additionalInvestigations: Targeted SACS genetic testing to confirm sacsin deficiency
MRI brain showing superior vermian atrophy, linear pontine hypointensities and pontine thickening
Fundoscopy and optical coherence tomography documenting retinal nerve fibre hypermyelination
Nerve conduction studies characterising the associated neuropathy
Exclusion of treatable recessive ataxias (e.g. vitamin E deficiency)
Broader recessive ataxia gene panel when SACS testing is inconclusive
redFlags: Rapid deterioration or new focal signs suggesting an alternative or superimposed process
Severe spasticity causing painful contractures and immobility
Recurrent falls with injury from combined ataxia, spasticity and sensory loss
Progressive dysphagia with aspiration risk in advanced disease
reference.prognosis: ARSACS is slowly progressive; ambulation is typically preserved into adulthood before wheelchair dependence develops in later life, and disability accrues from worsening spastic ataxia and neuropathy, though life expectancy is often only modestly reduced.
pitfalls: Attributing childhood spastic ataxia to cerebral palsy and omitting genetic evaluation
Overlooking retinal nerve fibre hypermyelination, a valuable and relatively specific clue
Missing the characteristic pontine MRI changes that support the diagnosis
Failing to test for treatable recessive ataxias before settling on ARSACS
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
